utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: May we continue where we left off yesterday afternoon. If you recall, we were discussing the subara or fur hat and the hat, the sesir. The subara or fur hat you said was worn by the man named Mitar Knezevic, do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what a subara looks like, and I also know what a hat is. The subara is the Serb hat, cap, that people from our parts wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One possibility was that you could draw what it looked like. Do you think that you could do that? Could you draw what it looks like? Have you got a piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And something to draw with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please in the upper part or on the left-hand side, shall we say, in the left-hand corner, would you draw what a subara looks like, what you think it looks like, and on the right, a hat or sesir.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the subara can be like this or it can be shorter. You can raise it up or make it shorter whereas a hat has a rim. I don't know actually how I'm going to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I had hoped that this would be done overnight, I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't had any contacts with Mrs. Vasiljevic for understandable reasons. She has taken the solemn declaration. Perhaps we could have told her at the end of yesterday's session to have a go, but I think that the explanation that she has given by saying that the hat or sesir has a rim whereas the subara type does not have a rim is something which is satisfactory for our purposes and that we can agree that one has a rim whereas the other hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you were thinking of the Russian-type hat with the ear flaps, but that's quite different. It's not that type of subara, the Russian type with the ear flaps, but you can raise it up and push it inside and it then can be short like a very short cap, hat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, provided that we agree that the word "rim" is the same as "brim," that the subara does not have a brim, then I think that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, sorry, Your Honour, "brim."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then we are agreed. Thank you, Mr. Domazet. I thought that we had been asked for it to be done overnight but if it wasn't clear, then it's my fault. But we've got, I think now, a clear picture of what it is to which she is referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, can you describe for us, to the best of your recollection, what the hat looked like that your husband wore from time to time at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hat that Mitar wore sometimes was smaller. It was a hunting hat, because his father was a hunter and had the hat. And so sometimes Mitar would use a smaller hat like that. It was a darker colour and with a small brim, narrow brim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Mrs. Vasiljevic, it is a hat with a small brim, of smaller dimensions, that is, and the colour was dark; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you remember - and I'm speaking of that time and that year, 1992 - whether, at that period which we have discussed at length, your husband, Mitar, wore a coat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar didn't own a coat, nor did he ever wear a coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you mean he didn't wear a topcoat or coat at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't have a topcoat, nor did he wear one ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Throughout the time that you have been married to your husband, did he ever wear a moustache?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. He never wore a moustache, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he ever have a beard?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never had a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, can you tell me who your kum was at the wedding ceremony when you married Mitar, that is to say, the first witness or the main kum, at your wedding ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our first witness and main kum at my wedding was Luka Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, did you hear about a wedding that took place after the war at which Milan Lukic was the main witness, or rather, kum? So my question to you is: Did you hear about a wedding of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Shall I try -- let me put it this way: Do you know somebody called Rade Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know Rade Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did his son get married in recent years?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, his son did get married, and he had a wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you personally invited to attend that wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. My husband attended the wedding, and so did my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Vasiljevic, when you spoke about the house you lived in, you spoke about the house which your father-in-law, that is to say, Mitar's father, bought, which you lived in, and you mentioned another house as well which, in the 1980s, you started building. Could you tell me now, please, whether, and if so, when, you ever completed the house for it to be habitable at all.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did complete the house in 1999, and SFOR lived in the house. They moved in, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So when you had made the house habitable, you did not move in, but the SFOR moved in and they rented the place from you as tenants; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. SFOR members lived in our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who drew up a contract with them about the lease and rent of the house?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether the money that was deposited by way of rent, was it a deposit to cover several months of rent in advance, or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They paid in advance for us to be able to finish what was left to do so that they could move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly: You received the money in advance to be able to complete the construction that hadn't been completed so that they could move in?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, for us to be able to complete the house and furnish it so that they could move in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you, please pause. You are both coming in on top of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If you count back from the arrest of your husband, how many months before that did SFOR come to rent your house, in addition to the old house that you yourselves lived in? How long before the arrest was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SFOR took up residence, I think, seven months before Mitar was arrested, seven months prior to Mitar's arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During that time, during those seven months, as you say, throughout that time, was Mitar there and did he live in the house next door to the SFOR building, the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all lived there, Mitar too. All of us were there. While SFOR was renting out our place, we were next door, all of us living in the house next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from living in the house next door, did he have any special relationships with the soldiers living there, that is to say, did he socialise or see them?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. They were all friends. Mitar socialised, our children did. We would go over to them when they had a birthday celebration, a birthday party, or their Christmas or New Year, and they would come to our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume that the SFOR people changed from time to time. Did they know that your husband's name was Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they did. All of them knew who we were and what we were and they all knew Mitar. Of course they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anybody ever, of any official organs of Republika Srpska or of SFOR tell your husband that there was the -- he was a suspect and that investigations were underway with respect to what had been going on during the war conflict and that he was a suspect in those investigations? Did anybody ever tell you that, anybody official in an official capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Nobody ever told me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since 1992 up until the beginning of the year 2000 when Mitar was arrested, did Mitar ever change his residence, place of residence at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Mitar never changed his place of residence. He was always there. He was never absent, not a single night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I say "changed residence," did he spend a period of time outside Visegrad, that's what I mean, and outside the house in Vojvode Stepe Street that you lived in all together?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mitar never changed his place of residence where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In talking to you, did he ever express any qualms or doubts that he might be arrested or that any proceedings might be initiated against him? Did he ever express any qualms of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. He never had any doubts along those lines, never suspected anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you, Mrs. Vasiljevic, present when he was arrested, and what were your reactions to that arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't at home at the time. I was working. My daughter came sometime around half past 3.00. Usually Mitar would go into town and come back home, he would do this several times, and she said, "Well, daddy hasn't come home yet. I don't know where he is."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In answer to some of my questions, you said that you worked as a tradesperson, salesperson in Visegrad and in several places around Visegrad; is that right? Did you work actually in villages inhabited either only by Muslims or where the majority of the population were Muslims because the surrounds of Visegrad are -- is made up of villages of different ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked in villages where the majority population were Muslims, and also in villages with a mixed population where there were Muslims and Serbs. I worked in Crnca where there was not a single house, they were all the Muslim houses, and I worked in town too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from Crnca which you said was an exclusively Muslim village, could you perhaps remember another village where there were mostly Muslims where you worked as a salesperson?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in Dusce, that's another one, mostly Muslims living in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned working in Prelovo, is Prelovo a mixed village with mixed inhabitants or is it a Serb village with Serb inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did work in Prelovo. There are Serbs living there, but I think that more of the -- most of the inhabitants are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you worked in those villages, how did you personally get on with the villagers who belonged to a different ethnic group or rather the Muslims in those villages?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had excellent relations with them. Nobody ever said anything to me and I didn't say anything -- I didn't have any problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That means, I take it, that you never had any problems. Did they have any problems with you, that is to say, did anybody complain to the company that employed you about your work or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, never. Nobody ever complained, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During all that time, did any of the Muslims ever complain to you about your husband Mitar, about his conduct towards Muslims which was not -- which they thought was not in order or anything like that, not proper?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever complained to me about Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Vasiljevic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, while we are talking about Prelovo, you said that there are mostly Muslims there. Do you mean that today, Prelovo is still comprised mostly of Muslims or did you mean that back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1992, they were Muslims. Today, it's a Serb-populated village because they haven't returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did the Muslims go?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they left when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet has asked you a number of questions about the SFOR personnel living in your house. They were French, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were French, and my children went to learn French with them. They gave them French classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And they remained in that house up until the time that your husband was arrested; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long after your husband had been arrested did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my husband was arrested, and when I came home, they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So from the moment your husband was arrested, they no longer lived in your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, surely you must realise at this stage that those men were there to arrest your husband, and lived in your house for six months in order to try to find out information about Milan Lukic. Certainly that must have occurred to you by this stage, no?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know anything about what they were doing there. All I knew was that they lived in my house. I have no idea why they lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You are aware now that the indictment against your husband was a sealed indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that later on when my husband left and when all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you now know that the indictment against your husband was in existence during the time that those French SFOR soldiers were living in your house. You now realise that to be true, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that now, but I didn't know that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said yesterday - and you were referring to Milan Lukic - you said: "I heard that he took part in house burning, but I don't know. I wasn't there. I didn't see it. Ugly things, but I don't remember what were all the things that he did." Can I ask you: When did you first learn that Milan Lukic had been involved in a house-burning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I remember correctly, these are the words which the witness did say, but with respect to another person, another person altogether, and not Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I didn't say that it was Milan Lukic. I said that it was Mitar Knezevic. That's what I heard. I didn't see it, but that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can check in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Milan Lukic; Mitar Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's certainly my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me clear that up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. That is my recollection of what she said. She was talking about Mitar Knezevic. There's no doubt about that, because I remember Mr. Domazet trying very hard and for a very long time to get some further information about him from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then I apologise for my misinterpretation of the record and I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you first heard that this person named Mitar Knezevic had been involved in a house-burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know when he became involved. Later on, stories started circulating around the town about him, and there were newspapers, but I don't know when he became involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would have been in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you remember who told you that Mitar Knezevic had been involved in a house-burning?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't. I don't. I read about it, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there were two house-burnings covered in the media from Visegrad. One was on Pionirska Street and one was in Bikavac. The rumour or the story that you heard regarding Mitar Knezevic, did it specify which house he was involved in the burning of?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rumour went that houses had been set on fire. There were different stories. I do not know which newspaper or who is it that wrote that it was Mitar Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, we know from other testimony in this case that many houses were set on fire. I understood you to mean yesterday that people died in the house-burning that you were referring to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who died, who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But the house-burning that you were referring to yesterday, was that a house-burning in which you believe people died?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only read about it in the newspaper afterwards. I read all sorts of things. Otherwise, I don't know anything, because I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I'm just trying to understand whether or not it was your belief that people died in the fire. Was it your belief or was it not your belief?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess so. I have no idea. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us that your husband owned one hat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't wear it all the time. At times, now and then, he would put on a smallish hat, but he didn't wear it always.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he only own one hat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't have any hats. At times he would borrow it from his father and wear it. He himself didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he had no hats, and the only hat that you ever saw him with was his father's hat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with a military-type hat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know what a military-type hat looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And certainly, you being his wife, if he had such a hat, would have seen it hanging in the house or have seen him wearing it at some point; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had it, nor did I ever see a military hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that nor did your husband own a coat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a heavy coat but not a light topcoat, not a raincoat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he had a heavy coat, as you're describing it now. Was that the only coat that he had?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Which do you mean? A jacket, a short coat; or a long one, a topcoat? Yes, he had both of these things, but he never had a light coat, a light, long coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you're telling us that your husband had two coats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course he had a number of jackets. He had a number of jackets. Coats, topcoats, no, he never had that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us the number of jackets that your husband had?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I mean, he worked as a waiter, so of course he had suits and he had jackets, and when he worked, he would have to wear a black suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's just confine ourselves to out door coats, something that somebody would wear over their clothing when they go outside. How many of -- how many jackets did he have meeting that description?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. He didn't have a mantle or any topcoat, anything that he would wear over his jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he would wear outside when it was raining?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wore the olive-green/grey uniform and his clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But he had no protection from the rain?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I mean, of course he had an umbrella. I don't see what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in the wintertime, when it gets cold in Visegrad, what kind of jacket or coat does he wear then?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course he must have had -- of course he had a winter jacket, a heavy jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the colour of that jacket?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still he has it. Well, it's a relatively light colour, short.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say "short," to what portion of his body does the coat reach?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, just like any other jacket. Just like a jacket, not a long one. Just a short -- like this. Like this, you know. A jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You're describing the jacket that you have now; correct? You're pointing to your jacket. Do you mean it's the same length as the jacket you have on here in Court?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Perhaps even shorter than what I have on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you describe what the witness is wearing, then? I'm afraid I've not seen the length of her coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The coat that you're wearing comes just below your waist; correct? The coat that you're wearing now, it comes just below your waistline; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. His jacket is shorter than the one that I'm wearing now. This one is longer than his jacket is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would his jacket come to his waistline? Is that what you're trying to describe for us?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'd say just an ordinary -- just an ordinary jacket, not a long one. Like this, relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you told us that one day your husband came home and he was quite distraught and he kept talking about a colleague and his colleague's son, and you told us, if I remember correctly, that that day -- on that day you had a birthday party for your son Nikola; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, you didn't get me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a birthday party for your son Nikola around that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. You did not understand what I was saying at all. What I said that Mitar's colleagues would come for Nikola's birthday, and Nikola's birthday was in August. It wasn't that day when Mitar was so distressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've told us a bit about Serbian custom. Is it Serbian custom to, on a child's birthday, have a party and invite friends of the family to that party?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I invite my colleagues, Mitar invites his, and we were preparing this -- when we had this party. There must have been about 10 of Mitar's colleagues and my colleagues, and all our close and distant relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While we're discussing Serbian custom, could you give me an idea, when would a typical Serbian family have their Sunday meal, what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sunday meal, well, depends. Depends on whether you're at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say a family that is at home.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take a family that is home, would they typically have the meal in the middle of the day or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it depends. Can be at 3.00, can be at 5.00, depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask about your family. What time would you typically prepare a Sunday meal for your children and your husband? What time would you prepare the Sunday meal?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends if we are all there, then -- I can't really say exactly. It depends when we are -- when we all get back home, when we're all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say that everybody is home, what time do you prepare your Sunday meal? Nobody is working, nobody is going anywhere, just the family is there, what time would you prepare the family meal?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Depends on where we all get together. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you mind telling us who was Nikola's Godfather?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikola's Godmother was Godmother kuma Smiljana Lukic. She was the one that christened him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: According to Serbian custom, does the child simply have a Godmother or a Godfather or would a child have both a Godmother and a Godfather?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Serb tradition, you start with your oldest kum and then you go down the line that is the oldest son and then younger, but Nikola had a Godmother because our kum Luka Lukic was in Austria and his mother was there alone, so we invited her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If Luka Lukic had been home, would your son have had a Godmother and a Godfather or simply a Godfather, Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, it would have been only Luka Lukic because it's men come first and only if there are no men or if he is ill or something then somebody else. You first start with men, and only then if no men are available, then you select a woman, then women's turn comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the relationship is between Smiljana Lukic and Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were Lukics. What they were one to another, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you don't know whether your kuma is Milan's aunt or mother or some other relationship; you're not able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that she's his aunt, seeing that her surname is Lukic so I guess she's his aunt or rather his father's brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is your daughter's Godfather?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it is Luka Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the birthday party for a second. You say that Meho Dzafic had been invited in previous years to birthday parties celebrated in your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a number of Mitar's colleagues, Hodzic Omer, a young one, Omer, an older one; Meho, I don't know, Sitni, I didn't even know what his true name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Meho --

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Meho accept these invitations and come to your house and celebrate birthday celebrations in your house?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you give us an approximate number of how many times Meho was at your house at these birthday celebrations?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once, perhaps, for a birthday party, but otherwise, he came sometimes he just came to see Mitar. At times he would give Mitar a ride back home and -- depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me or would you say that he was at your house more than once or twice a month, that he would stop by your house?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times. They all dropped by or came along with Mitar but I just don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I correctly assume that Meho's family would have returned the invitation and would have invited you and your husband to a birthday or other celebrations in his family; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They never invited -- Mitar usually invited his colleagues and I usually invited mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I asked you was: Were you ever invited to a birthday party that Meho was hosting for somebody in his family?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I never went. I don't know if Mitar did. I know that he was his colleague but I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the names of Meho's children?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the name of Meho's wife?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the street that Meho lived on?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Mitar knows it, perhaps, because they worked together. Perhaps Mitar knows his children and him, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what car Meho drove?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho had a white, a small white Fiat, Fiat 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday a bit more about this kum relationship and you described for us very vividly the strength of this kum bond. At one point you told us that if one breaks this kumship, then it is believed in Serbian tradition that bad things will befall the family that breaks this kumship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the old -- this was an old kumship, I don't know, 100 or 200 years. And according to our custom, there must be certain ceremonies if a kum needs to be changed, that you have to ask your former kum, but it's not good to change your kum. And as long as we live, Vasiljevic and Lukic will always be kums. They will never separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in when I heard you yesterday when you said that you believe that if that kum relationship were to be severed, that that would bring bad luck or bad fortune upon the Vasiljevic family. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to some traditional beliefs, that is not even permitted. It is not permitted to sever this kind of relationship, and if you do, yes, then ill luck will strike you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that in your mind, the Vasiljevic family and the Lukic family are still in this kum relationship; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, of course. We've never broken it. But it need not mean because we are living on and we have our offspring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your opinion, so let me ask for specifically, in your opinion, is your husband still a kum of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, of course. Of course he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is he still a kum with Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see if I have this correct, your husband has told us that Milan Lukic has done some terrible things and that according to him, your husband has been wrongfully accused of a crime he believes Milan Lukic committed, one of the most horrific crimes in the conflict. You have lost your husband for almost two years, you've lost the benefit of his wages for two years, your children have lost their father for two years, and it is still your belief that your family and the Lukic family are kum?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we never broke our relations. It doesn't mean that we shall be with Milan Lukic, but our children and his children, these ties, these bonds were never severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And one of the reasons they will never sever is because you believe bad things will happen to your family if that relationship is severed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to our belief, that is not good. It is not advisable to change your kum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, your husband is facing a charge for which he could receive a very lengthy sentence. Do you sincerely believe that this kum relationship must persist despite all that has happened at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it will go on. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that in the Uzice hospital, that a man from Visegrad shared the room with your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several of them. There were people who had been there before my husband. There were a number of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just interested in the people from Visegrad who were in the room at the same time as your husband. How many people from Visegrad were in that same room?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a man whose first name was Dragan, and another one -- and he was from Visegrad, and there was a Muslim, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that Muslim man was from Visegrad as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. I don't know. I don't know where he came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But Dragan was from Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. That Dragan was killed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us his last name?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name was Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you know why he was in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He sustained some injury, whether his arm or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when did he die?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, after he was released from the hospital, later on I heard that he was killed. I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the day that your husband had this accident and broke his leg, you told us that you were home the entire day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had a day off that day, because we usually set it at the company level when would which shop be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you told us that this was the Feast of the Holy Trinity. Was your shop open that day and you just didn't work, or was the shop closed on that Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, there is a schedule, so one shop is open on Monday and closes on Tuesday, and so on and so forth. And that particular day, I was having a day off because our shop had a day off; that is, it was closed that day. All the other shops were open and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What shop were you working in at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the supermarket, on the square.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And even it being Holy Trinity Sunday, the other shops in Visegrad town, you're saying, were open that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were, some weren't. It depended on the schedule, because that's how we worked. Some would be open on Sundays, others wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who would make up this schedule? Who would decide which store should be open on a particular day and which store should be closed?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in our company, the management. I worked in a state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so in 1992, your company was still owned by the state?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you told us that you first learned that your husband had been injured from your uncle, when your -- or I believe your husband's uncle called on the phone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. His uncle called me, his mother's brother, his uncle, not his father's brother. His mother's brother, that kind of uncle, on his ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is the man whose son was killed recently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know where he was when he called you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at home in Vardiste, and that's where he phoned me from, from his own house, because they stopped in the car that Mitar was in. There was a driver and somebody else, and he called me and said that Mitar had fallen off a horse and broken his leg. They gave him a blanket to cover him up because he was cold, it was raining. And of course, they took me off to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around what time did you receive that phone call?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what time it was exactly, but it was just before dark, at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And before that -- well, that was the first way in which you learnt; you heard nothing before that about your husband's accident. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it would seem, then, that all of the people, some of them friends of your husband's, that came to his aid at the place where he fell off the horse, none of those people called you to tell you that he had been hurt; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. Correct. Nobody called me before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we've heard testimony that he was in the Visegrad hospital for a period of time, being x-rayed and being attended to. During that period of time, nobody from the hospital called you to tell you that your husband was injured? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't. Nobody called. Probably they took him to hospital, and perhaps they didn't have enough petrol or cars. You know, it was wartime. So nobody called me except the uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know -- or can you tell us where it was that your husband fell off the horse?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me later on. It was in the square, Visegrad square, opposite the hotel, opposite the Visegrad hotel, in front of the garden and grill. But there's the Panos terrace grill. This was the other one, the UPI terrace grill, garden grill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So was there a time -- and it's been almost nine years now - has there been a time now that you have walked through that square with your husband and perhaps your children, and your husband has said to you, "That is where that old horse slipped and I fell"?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know where it is, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did your husband point out the precise spot where the horse slipped and fell?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't actually go, but I know where it is, round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that the witness be handed a blank piece of paper. I've put "P107" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're going to ask you to draw something again. I'm going to ask you just to draw a representation of the square, whatever shape it is. We're not looking for scale or for accuracy. Just draw a representation of the square.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, more or less. This is the furniture store. I don't know exactly, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to draw a circle and put an "X" in it to indicate where it was that your husband told you he had the accident with the horse.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you put a circle with an "X" in it to mark that spot? Before it goes onto the ELMO, can I ask you to draw a number "1" over the spot that you said was the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned UPI coffee shop, I believe. Can you put a number "2" to show us where it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was the UPI terrace grill, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The UPI terrace grill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you put the number "3" to show --

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you put the number "3" to show us where the Visegrad hotel is.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visegrad [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that be placed on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an Expres fast-food thing and a department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to put a "4" to indicate where this Expres fast food is located and to put a "5" to show us where the department store is located.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] No. That's where the fire brigade was. You want the department store? Well, that's the square, the fountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Before it goes back on the ELMO, just to be clear: So you've put a "4" to indicate where the Expres fast-food shop is?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "4" is the Expres, next to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And you've put a "5" to show us where the department store is?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the snack bar is actually in the department store. The department store is here, and the snack bar is within the department store somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there a number 5 to show us where the department store is?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One moment. The snack bar is a new phrase, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: She's saying that's inside number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But which snack bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us which snack bar you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the department store, up on the floor above. In the department store upstairs, there's a sort of cafe or snack bar. Downstairs is the department store, and the snack bar is upstairs, in the department store upstairs. The Expres is something separate, there's the Expres or fast food, and there's the snack bar in the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've told us about three places to eat. The UPI grill, the Expres food and the snack bar, those are three separate places?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the hotel, and the Visegrad hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we finish up, can you just write your name on the bottom of that piece of paper to indicate that it's you who's made that drawing. Just write your name on the bottom, the very bottom. It's not over anything you've marked already. Perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO for us to see. Just so we're clear, the X that you marked to indicate where your husband indicated he fell from the horse, it's just to the left of the number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps I haven't drawn it accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, there are two 5s now on the drawing. I don't know whether you keep a list of the instructions you give somebody to do one of these complicated drawings, but the 5 as the snack bar is the last name we used the number 5, but there's a 5 up there next to the "RX".

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe that's the department store and the snack bar is in side the department store and I'll just rely on the record for a description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you. It's not clear to me, but I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the number 5 indicates both the location of the department store and the snack bar that's contained in the department store; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department store, and upstairs is the snack bar. It's the same building. One is upstairs, the department store is downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would tender that now as Prosecution Exhibit P107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have no objections that the diagram be admitted, but Mr. Groome said that the witness, that Mitar had shown her the place. She said that he had described the place, but never actually pointed it out to her on the spot. So I'd like to clear that up. I have nothing against the diagram and sketch being admitted into evidence as being the place that she considers, according to his description, that that was the place because I understood her to say that he had described the place.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never there. I didn't actually see it for myself, but he told me where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, we'll get on a lot more quickly if you don't talk over counsel, please. What Mr. Domazet said is quite correct, but I don't think it destroys the document as a document. It will be Exhibit P107.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, I'd like to return now to the Sunday of the accident. What time did your husband leave the house that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mitar left in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it before or after you got up from your bed?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not straight after he got up, of course. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, had you arisen for the day and -- had the children had breakfast? Can you tell us whether it was before or after the children had had their breakfast?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't remember actually what -- when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about your particular shop, the company that owned your particular shop, sometimes it would be open, and sometimes it would be closed depending on the schedule. Your shop was a food shop; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the town of Visegrad, there are many, many different types of shops; correct? Some would sell clothes, some would sell books; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not many shops, just five or six. There are more food stores, but otherwise, just one shop for each thing. It's a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And these other shops, can you give us an idea of the shops that aren't food shops, what do they sell?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know at that time which were open, which were actually working at that time. Some were on duty, open on Sundays, some were open on Mondays, particularly for bread. The bread stores were open. Supplies weren't that plentiful either so there weren't that many goods in the shops. There aren't many now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that the stores that -- any stores that would have been open on that Sunday would have been the shops like you describe, perhaps selling bread or milk or essential food that people would need on a Sunday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bakeries were open selling bread, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your husband off from work that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband would go off for an hour or two to clean the town, and that's what he did that day too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So on this Holy Trinity Sunday, your husband did leave to clean the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's that got to do with it? Had it been a saint day of ours, our own personal family saint day, he might not have gone. But otherwise, everybody would work normally. Those assigned would do so. If it was our family holy saint day or if we had been digging or constructing our house he might not have gone, but as it's not our family holiday, wouldn't go. Now, a family actually celebrating the Holy Trinity as their own family saint day, then they would not go, but otherwise if it wasn't your personal family saint, you could go to work. We celebrate, for example, St. George's Day so we wouldn't go to work on that day, whereas other people who wouldn't have a family St. George's day would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your husband wasn't paid for this work, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you make a dinner that day? Did you cook dinner for your family?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what time did you plan to serve the dinner that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know because of what happened to Mitar, so I don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've forgotten because of the accident?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We probably had dinner sort of a late meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would he have been there for that meal?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably he would have because it was a late meal, a little later than we would usually eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea of when you say "late meal," around what time of the day would you consider it to be a late meal?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, late is 8.00, but this might have been before, a little before 8.00 when I heard the news. I think it was 7.00 or 8.00. After that, it would be too late for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Mitar was present when your family ate that day; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From the time he left in the morning, did you see him again that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He would go in and out several times. Now, what happened that day, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is possible that he returned home after finishing his cleaning and then went out again; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember because sometimes during a day, he would go out and work for an hour or two and come back home and then leave again. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where would he go when he would leave again?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he'd come home, have a bit of a rest sometimes. Sometimes he'd have some odd job to see to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you expecting your husband home for the meal that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you first know who Milan Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that Milan Lukic existed, but I had never seen him before the war broke out and before I heard that he had come to Visegrad. I think as soon as the Uzice Corps came, then, I am not quite sure. He suddenly turned up in Visegrad around that time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you married your husband, how old would you say Milan Lukic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know him then at all, nor was he around. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me go back to this kum relationship again. At the time that you were married, your family or Mitar's family and the Lukics were in this kum relationship. My question is: Would it not be natural to assume that Milan Lukic probably, whatever age he was, perhaps a teenager at the time, was at your wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He's much younger than us, at least 15 years, about 15 years younger than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any family celebrations over the years prior to the Uzice Corps arriving in Visegrad that you can recall seeing Milan Lukic at one of the family celebrations?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sredoje was in Visegrad. That's where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you see him at different family celebrations?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps for our Slava, family holy day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he attend your wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just another point on Serb traditions, isn't it correct that there are actually two parts to a Serbian wedding? The first part in the registrar office, the government office, and then the second part in the orthodox church presided over by the priest; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but we didn't have a big wedding. We just had the ceremony at the registry. We never got married in church. It's not obligatory. You don't have to. You don't have to get married in church after the civil ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Milan Lukic ever have the second part of his wedding ceremony, the part of the ceremony in the church? Are you aware of him ever having that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't think -- I don't believe he married in church. I don't think he had a church ceremony as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to Milan Lukic's wedding, did your husband ever express reservations about being his best man?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Milan didn't even have a wedding. He got married, and Mitar was the witness at the registry, just for an hour or two. That's what he told me, that it was all very quick. They just went to the registry office to get married. It all lasted a short time. He didn't make an actual wedding, big wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after the wedding, or the day of the wedding, did he come and tell you what happened that day, that Milan Lukic had been married that day? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but as he was talking, he said that Milan asked him in passing. As a rule, he should have invited his father, but his father lived a long way away. There was no transport. I think Mitar's father was ill. And then he got to know Mitar, who is the eldest son of the father. And it just took one or two hours in the registry office. Whether they went to have lunch or not after that, I don't know, but it was all very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you ever seen photographs from Milan Lukic's wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There weren't any. There was no photographing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your husband ever express reservations or concerns that he had after the wedding, telling you something to the effect that he didn't want to be his best man but he felt he was obliged to? Did he ever say something in substance like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't feel the same way as he had earlier on, but that's how it had to be, following on from the tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what he said to you after he was the best man at Milan's wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say anything special. He just said he met him and that he asked him to do this. He couldn't refuse, of course, because he couldn't call anybody else. His brother was in Belgrade, and the others were I don't know where, so he couldn't refuse him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the baptism of Milan's child, who from your family attended that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My Mitar and Marina and Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why was it that you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Probably I had to go to work or something like that, because I was the only breadwinner. Nobody else was working at that time, so I had to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it true your husband never returned to work at the Panos restaurant after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he started working in one of Panos's smaller catering establishments, a smaller restaurant that they owned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.28 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, just before the break, we were talking about your husband working at Panos. My question to you is after he was -- after he got out of the hospital, did he return to work in the Panos -- or work for the Panos company?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He returned to Panos in -- could have been late 1992, end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he work for the Panos company up until the time of his arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he stop working for the Panos company?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. He quit because they were not paying any salaries or anything, so he worked for a while, for a rather short while, and then he simply quit because -- and they were not paying out any salaries or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say her name was? I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In case my pronunciation isn't 100 per cent correct, the person I'm asking about is a person whose name is Behija Zukic who owned a shop with her husband. Do you know the person who I'm referring to? I believe your husband told us that the shop was on the way home from Visegrad to your house.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I did know her from about the shop. She had her own shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you ever go to that shop to buy groceries?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, a number of witnesses have told us about a car that she had, a red Passat, that it seemed that many if most of the people in Visegrad recognised as being owned by her. Are you familiar with this red Passat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know who had what car. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you do not know what car Behija Zukic had, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. No, no. I didn't know it. I knew her but I didn't know anybody else, not her husband, nor her children. Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions now regarding your husband's alcoholism. When would you say he first had a problem with drinking?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he always drank, and he would always be in trouble when he drank for longer periods of time, and of course he eats nothing when he drinks and then, of course, we have to go to the doctor. Even before, I believe he was treated for alcoholism sometime in the 1980s, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he have this problem before you were married?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really know how about before, but he had this problem ever since we were married. You know, he doesn't drink and then he goes on a drinking bout and drinks for five or six days, and then he eats nothing and of course he loses weight so he has to go to the doctor to get an infusion to recover, start eating again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anything that you were able to do when he was in one of these drinking bouts? Was there anything that you were able to do to help him get out of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why of course, but he could not even take any food in. So he did need this infusion to recover a little because when he consumed alcohol, he simply did not eat anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in thinking that when he was on one of these drinking bouts, that he would spend some of his wages on alcohol?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was very sociable so he liked company, he'd stay with them and he'd spend the money, but then he would make up for it by working, and that is what he did. He would work more until he made up for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was his drinking, did it ever create a financial hardship for you and your children?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that we were indifferent to it, but he always tried to make up for all that to somehow make amends for what he's lost, for what he's spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How often would he go on these drinking binges?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did drink for a while, and then he wouldn't drink anything for some months and then he would start drinking again and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times a year would he have these drinking bouts?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends. Sometimes five or six months would go by without any alcohol, sometimes those intervals were shorter. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the times when he was drinking a lot, was it possible for you to reason with him? Could you discuss a matter with him about the children or perhaps about the house? Was it possible to discuss something with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, of course. In the beginning, it wasn't easy at all, I mean when he drank excessively, but then he'd stop drinking and everything would be back to normal. He wasn't aggressive or anything. Yes, we could talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever have a disagreement with him while he was drunk?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he ever shout at your children while he was drunk?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he doted on his children. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From what you're telling us now, it seems that the only real problem with your husband's drinking is that he stopped eating and would lose weight. Other than that, it doesn't seem that it had much impact on the family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite, quite. Nothing else. It was only bad for him, because his health would deteriorate and at times he would ramble, so that he would have to go to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your primary concern was not so much for anything he might do; it was simply for his own physical health. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because it was bad for him. He was running himself into trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to May and June of 1992. Did there come a time when everything you've described now changed, that now your husband's behaviour seemed somewhat different to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would be a change, like sometimes when he could not bear something; for instance, when he was in the hospital and saw those wounded men without arms, without legs, and then he would be quite distraught. I mean, he could not bear that, and I could see it in his behaviour that he really was very unhappy when he saw things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd actually ask you to focus on the time period before he went into the hospital. Did there come a time when you noticed, let's say somewhere at the beginning of June, a dramatic change in his behaviour that concerned you very much?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. He started drinking more when his cousin Zeljko was killed. He changed then. He was very cut up, because that cousin was his father's single son, so that he mourned him truly, he cried a lot, could not come down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did that change in behaviour remain up until the time that he went into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was always quite upset when something like that happened. He would be less coherent when he was distressed by something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say "less coherent," do you mean it was more difficult to have a discussion with him about something that you needed to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not that it was more difficult, but he would -- he could not properly focus when he would be cut up by one of such things. Then he'd really feel it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you call him -- would you consider him as having been depressed after the death of his cousin?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, he was depressed. He cried for days on end. He somehow could not accept that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you consider that he became more aggressive after his cousin died?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you consider him perhaps excitable or agitated at the time after his cousin died?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. Perhaps slightly more nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After his cousin died, did you notice that perhaps he was staying out for long periods of time and not returning home? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. He liked to go, to leave, and then come back. There was only once that for about two or three days I didn't know where he was, so I asked around, and I was told that he was at Uzamnica and that he was on a hunger strike. It was then that he did not come back and that I was told that he had been detained there, that he had been disarmed, that he wasn't eating, so that a doctor or a nurse, or whoever it was, went up there to administer a drip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So between the time that his cousin died and the time that he went into hospital, other than this period of two or three days, he would come home every night and there was nothing that concerned you about his behaviour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
