utterances.text: Well, then, when his cousin was killed, it could have been a day later that he returned home, quite disturbed. He was very shaken when he mentioned his colleague, but he was really -- he was really making no sense, so that I couldn't really understand what he was trying to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's put aside for a second what he may have told you. From the time that he's released from Uzamnica up until the time that he goes into the hospital - and according to him, that seems to be about two weeks, from the 1st or the 2nd to the 14th - during that two-week period, was he coming home at night?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He continued to clean the town then, going away for an hour or two. They would clean the town, and after that he would come back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there anything during that two-week period about his behaviour that caused you concern, that made you worry, anything at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, I want to read you a portion of your husband's medical record, and then after I read it, I'm going to ask you a few specific questions. "Wife's description of case history: 'He used to drink a lot of alcohol but was never aggressive. Since the beginning of the fighting, he has always been engaged, agitated, impatient. He is always going somewhere and remains in the unit, even when his shift is over. He was particularly upset by the death of a close relative.'" Now, the question I have for you is: Did you tell a doctor who was treating your husband in Uzamnica hospital that your husband seemed engaged?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "engaged"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the word that the doctor wrote in the statement. Do you remember using any word of that nature when discussing your husband's condition with the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he was treated by orthopaedic surgeons. I suppose he could not simply watch those people who were around him, because they were people from Bajna Basta, from Zvornik, from Visegrad, the wounded, and I suppose he simply couldn't bear to look at them any more, so they moved him from the orthopaedic ward to the other ward, I suppose. Something must have disturbed him there, shaken him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the portion of the medical record that I just read to you doesn't indicate that you said your husband was incoherent or not making sense, but that it says that you told the doctor that he was engaged, agitated, impatient? You'd agree with me that there's nothing about being incoherent in that portion that I read?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no. No, no, no. No. He must have been affected, disturbed by certain things that happened there, I mean where he was -- the room he was in. I can't remember the words that I used then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you tell the doctor that he was agitated?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I said to the doctor. I only could see that he was in a poor shape, that they were giving him sleeping pills, that he looked very exhausted, and that is when I asked that he be released home, because at that time there was a shortage of medicines, even at the hospital. So at home I had to look for those medicines. Then there was a shortage of food, because there were wounded from all over the place, and that was why I asked to take him home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever tell the doctor that your husband was impatient?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it says also that you stated, "He is always going somewhere." What did you mean by that, "He is always going somewhere"?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, when did I say that? When, to whom did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a note from a doctor contained in your husband's case history. I don't have the exact date in front of me, but my best memory is that it's around July of 1992 is the time when the doctor made this note. Did you ever tell a doctor treating your husband, "He is always going somewhere"?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I think it was the doctor who said that because it was the doctor who wrote his case history. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the original please be placed on the ELMO for interpreter's sake?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not the witness who has to see it, it's the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're asking that it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that means it goes on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would just ask the interpreters is it the portion that they need to see visible on the ELMO at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The bit that you are reading, that's what they need it for. That's why they usually are given copies of this when you are cross-examining on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for not having done that, Your Honour, but as I do not speak B/C/S I'm unable to know if the portion -- but the entire page is not visible on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, no. That was not the fragment that was read by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May we simply give this exhibit to the interpreters so that they may find the portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be much easier for them, certainly, except that they'd have to share it then. There is more than one interpretation going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The case manager is making a copy. Maybe we'll go on to the final area and then come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, copies are being made of the original document to be sure that we're using the precise words that the doctor wrote down. I want to ask you about two events. I want to draw your attention to around the 18th of May, and I'm going to be asked that you be shown the pseudonym sheet, P106. I'm going to draw your attention to VG81. Is it your testimony that at no time in May or around that period of time that that witness was not stopped in front of your house by your husband, in your presence, and a conversation took place between you? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year, May, May, which year, 1992 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that person, nor did I ever come out. I know the person, but I did not come out, nor was I having any argument with that person at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to another name on that list, VG13. Do you see that person's name?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you know that person as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that person at all. Maybe I might but, no, I don't, I don't know this name. I wouldn't know that person by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say you might, do you think you know that person or you're pretty sure that you do not know that person?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now when I look at it, I just do not know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG13 states that sometime last year, you called her up and you asked her or, I'm sorry, you offered her money if she would not testify against your husband in this trial, and she also stated that you told her that you had spoken to VG18 on that list and had convinced her not to testify. Did that phone conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what Mr. Groome has just said, one could interpret it as if the witness VG13 said that here in the courtroom, and I truly cannot remember it ever being mentioned during the trial or during the testimony of that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I agree with you that there was no reference in that witness' evidence, but I don't think that the question or the sense of the question depends upon where VG13 said it. It is always better, if I may say so, Mr. Groome, that these sorts of allegations are put directly rather than trying to attribute them to somebody. It causes confusion, and it isn't really the point you're trying to make. You are accusing her of doing this. It's got nothing to do with VG13. Anyway, she has denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, did you ever contact VG18 and say anything to that witness, and that witness' name is on the list before you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea where that person is. I wouldn't know which -- where to call that person, which town, which city to call to find that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to go back to the medical record. The interpreters now have a copy so we can use the precise language that the doctor wrote. And I'll go back to the first description of "engaged," and I'll trust that they'll give you the exact word that is written in the record. Did you ever say to the doctor that your husband was engaged?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "engaged"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I presume that the interpreters have just used the precise word that the doctor noted. Did you ever use that word when describing your husband?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I was asked to describe it or was it up to that doctor to describe the state of his health. I presume that the case history must have been written by the doctor, not by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, may I suggest that you will get a lot further that you cease to attribute to this witness the word "engaged." It's a very medical term. What you have to put to her is did she ever suggest anything which suggests that he was able to reason or to converse, whatever meaning you seek to attribute to the word "engaged." It doesn't purport to be a verbatim statement by this witness. It's a medical history and doctors, unfortunately, use words quite differently to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's why I'm simply asking her did she use the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have now. But up to this stage, you have kept on ascribing to her the use of the word "engaged." Now, if you want to get somewhere, may I suggest you put your meaning on it and ask her whether she said anything -- I don't know, I haven't looked it up in the medical dictionary, but if you have a particular meaning to the word "engaged," that you seek to have attributed to the witness, ask her if she said anything along the words of whatever that meaning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no particular meaning to the word other than Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to rely on the official translation of the word she used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: She didn't use it. Now, there's no suggestion that she used it. She's denied it. There's nothing on the document to suggest she's used it. It's a medical history. A medical history is something that puts down in the doctor's understanding of terms. Now, if you want to get somewhere, I'm trying to assist you to get somewhere on this, use what you suggest is the meaning. If you have no meaning and she's denied the use of the word, we're not going to get anywhere by continually asking her the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the word "impatient," and I'd ask you to use the ordinary sense of that word, not a medical term. Did you ever describe your husband in the ordinary sense of the word as impatient?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was impatient. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever describe your husband --

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? Where was he impatient, in hospital? Was impatient in hospital, do you mean? It depends whether he was waiting for something to happen and then was impatient or -- because if he was ill and impatient in hospital, that's something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever describe your husband as being impatient in the period before his hospitalisation? Did you ever describe him as being that way to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever describe your husband to a doctor using the ordinary sense of the word "agitated"? Did you ever describe your husband as being that prior to his hospitalisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I said anything like that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever tell a doctor that your husband was always going somewhere prior to his hospitalisation: "He is always going somewhere"? Did you ever say that to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I told a doctor that. I don't know whether it had anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified just a few minutes ago that in the time period between your husband's cousin dying and the time that he went into the hospital, that he came home every night except the two or three days he was in Uzamnica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't know where he was for two or three days, until they told me. They told me that he was in detention in Uzamnica and was refusing food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is the doctor mistaken when he has a note saying "wife's description," and it says: "He is always going somewhere"? Is that an inaccurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he wrote down. I don't know what I actually said to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know what you actually said. I can only tell you what is actually written down, and what's written down is: "He is always going somewhere." Did you ever say that to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. I don't remember what I said, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever say to the doctor: "He remains in the unit even when his shift is over"? Did you ever tell a doctor that your husband remained in a unit even when his shift was over?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You never referred to his cleaning crew as a unit, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I don't know who worked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, at this period of time, this two-week period, he was not working other than the cleaning crew; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He just cleaned the town, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, isn't it a fact that you did say to the doctor: "He remains in the unit even when his shift is over," and that the unit you were referring to is Milan Lukic's unit, a unit of the White Eagles? Isn't that the truth of what you said to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Mitar was never with them, nor did I ever say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Vasiljevic, from Mr. Groome's question, there were some slight problems, perhaps because of the different terminology used in the English language or perhaps for some other reason. Could you explain to us, when you said that Mitar never wore a mantle or topcoat, when you said that, could you explain to us which coat you had in mind, what you mean when you say "mantle" coat, light coat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I come from, a coat is if you put -- if you -- say you have a suit on and a shirt and a tie, then when you get dressed up like that, you would put a coat over it, that type of coat that we call mantil. I don't know if you understand me. And he never had one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you explain to us briefly the difference between what we call a kaput, or great coat, and mantil, a lighter form of coat, as both these items of clothing are long. But there is a difference in our conception of them, is there not? And I think that we shall explain to the Court what we mean if we describe this.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A kaput is a kaput. A mantil is lighter in weight, perhaps longer. I don't know how to explain the difference. One that you put on over a suit when you get dressed up that way. Mitar never owned one. He had the jackets, men's jackets that you wear in winter, and that kind of thing, and a lighter jacket when the weather wasn't so cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Domazet, you may find yourself in the witness box very shortly. Are we talking about something such as a difference between an overcoat and a skiing jacket? I'm trying to get the sense of the way you described it, you see, without having to put you in the witness box to give it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A skiing jacket is something that is thicker, yes, but it is short in length, the length of a jacket to a suit, whereas the kaput and the mantil are longer, like what I'm wearing, perhaps a little shorter, but there is a difference. The witness said thinner, lighter, and I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Madam Vasiljevic, when you say "thinner" or "lighter," which of the two things, if you have a kaput and a mantil, which is thinner and lighter? Which is made from a thinner and lighter --

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the kaput is much thicker, longer, worn in winter, whereas the mantil type is thinner, lighter in weight, and you wear it over a suit. And Mitar never had one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have tried to clarify that point sufficiently and to get an answer. Thank you. Asked another question by Mr. Groome about your kums and the kums to your children, you said that one child was christened by Smiljana Lukic because Luka Lukic, the wedding kum, was not able to come, whereas the second child was christened by Luka Lukic. I should like to try to ask you to remember exactly which child was christened by Smiljana Lukic and which child was christened by Luka Lukic? Which of your two children had which kums?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I said exactly, but Marina was christened by kum Smiljana and Nikola was christened by kum Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Vasiljevic, asked by Mr. Groome about who came to your son's birthday parties or which colleagues Mitar would bring home from time to time, you enumerated several colleagues, you gave several names, and from that I gather that those several people were Muslims, judging by their names - I say that, "judging by their names" - and that among them you mentioned Meho Dzafic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were ten or so colleagues, about ten colleagues. I don't know exactly whether Meho was among them, but I think he was. I know that Hodzic, Agic, a man named Omer, they came. I forget the others. I know there was a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mrs. Vasiljevic, that there were a number of them, and you go on to enumerate Hodzic, Agic, Omer, and so on - just a moment, please. Let me finish, please, Madam - were they your husband's colleagues who were Muslims, of Muslim ethnicity? Is that right? Could you give me a yes or no answer, please. That will facilitate matters.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were Muslim -- of Muslim ethnicity. There were others, too, but I can't remember the names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the three men you mentioned, as well as Meho Dzafic, who you spoke about? Were they colleagues of your husband who would come by to your house with him from time to time, whom he would bring home from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all Mitar's colleagues who came by from time to time. There were others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Groome also asked you whether you knew their wives, or rather, the wife of Meho Dzafic, whether you knew Meho Dzafic's wife. Now, let me ask you: On those occasions when your husband brought his colleagues home, did he bring their wives home as well or did they come only on their own, themselves, just the husbands?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the husbands. Their wives did not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In mentioning the Uzice hospital and your going, can you remember how many times you went to the hospital while your husband was lying in Uzice hospital? And I'm thinking about 1992 when I say that. Do you happen to remember how many times you went?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Twice, I think, to the orthopaedics ward, and once when they put him into the ordinary daily ward.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could the witness repeat the latter half of her answer? "Once ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So twice to the orthopaedics and once to the neurological department. Was this a visit to the neurological department, and the fourth time when you took him out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that means three visits and once when you came to take him home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the interpreters missed the reference, if it was to the neurological department. They stated at the time the witness was answering it that they could not hear the end of her answer. You heard it as neurological department, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, for the interpreters and the transcript, please, would you repeat. Apart from the two visits to the orthopaedics ward, your next visit was to what ward?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'll use the right term medically, neuropsychiatry or neurology. Neuropsychiatry, I think it was, to the neuropsychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but it was the ward he was in after he left the orthopaedics ward; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Asked by Mr. Groome, Mrs. Vasiljevic, about the stores and shops which were open on Sundays, I think you explained that some stores were open, others were not, and on that particular Sunday that you were asked about, was the Holy Trinity holiday. Now, I want to ask you this: Were shops open generally on religious holidays such as the one in question, and are there any religious holidays when shops were shut because it was a religious holiday?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the management decided when shops would be open and when not. The Holy Trinity holiday is one that lasts three days. So I don't know who determined this, but I know that they decide which shop is going to be open on the first day of the holiday, and that would be the shop selling food, food stores and bakeries. Then for the second day of holidays, somebody else would be on duty, other shops would be open, and the same applied to the third day of the holiday depending on what the management, what schedule the management had made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. But let us go back and speak about the time before that, not in the last nine years, but the time up until 1992, including 1992. Did state holidays exist, holidays prescribed by the state when nobody goes to work?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We did have state holidays, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During those state holidays, and in addition to the state holidays, were there religious holidays that were also deemed to be state holidays when people didn't go to work? Let me rephrase that question. Do you remember up until 1992 which state holidays were celebrated in the country at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't work for the New Year, we didn't work for the 29th of November holiday, the 7th of July holiday, the 4th of July holiday, and maybe several years. I can't, perhaps, remember them all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope that I won't be leading if I ask you whether May 1st -- the 1st of May was a holiday, the state holiday too?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the 1st of May, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So those, then, were all the state holidays celebrated in the country at that time. Was there a religious holiday amongst those state holidays that you've just mentioned; were any of them religious?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we just didn't usually go to work. If somebody was celebrating his own family holiday, he would get a day off. Now, if there were four of us working, my colleagues, then if one of the ladies had her own family holiday, she would get a day off and not come to work that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, yes, I know what you're saying that for the Slava, the family religious holiday, it was provided by law that each person could ask for a free day to celebrate his family holiday, but I'm asking you about the state holidays now that which were the New Years, the 4th -- 1st of May, the 4th of May, and the 7th of May and the 29th of November -- sorry, the 4th of July and the 27th of July. Were any of those dates religious holidays or were they only state holidays?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Up until 1992, was it a state holiday? Was the orthodox Christmas a state holiday, did one -- did you go to work or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we never worked for Christmas, but I can't remember on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But before 1992, you state that you didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Christmas was always a holiday. All Serbs celebrated it and didn't go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, I can, perhaps, agree with you that all Serbs celebrated it, but I am asking you whether it was an official state holiday prescribed by the state? Did the state prescribe, and I'm talking about up to 1992, that there was no work on Christmas. Was that a state-prescribed holiday?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the Serbs worked then. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Muslims worked, for example, on that holiday?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it a state holiday then or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 4th of July was a state holiday with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Now, as the Holy Trinity day holiday is an orthodox holiday and a Slava, asked by Mr. Groome -- in answer to Mr. Groome's question you said that yes, it is an orthodox holiday but that it wasn't your Slava. Had it been your Slava, you would have celebrated it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, which is your Slava or the Slava observed by Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our Slava is St. George's day on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that day called differently amongst the Serbs, is it called -- is another term used to denote that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Djurdjevdan or St. George's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it is Djurdjevdan?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that is the Slava for which everybody could take a day off and not go to work and that that was customary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Today is the 16th of November. Is there a well-known Slava celebrated today?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which Slava is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's Djurdjic, I don't know. I know there are two that come up very close to each other around this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, it is Mr. Tanaskovic's Slava, but he has to work today.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you mean to say to Mr. Groome that as the Holy Trinity was not your family Slava, you had no particular obligations or responsibilities, nor as is customary did you invite guests home?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If it is your own personal family Slava, then you don't go to work. Otherwise, you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you explained all these customs and religious holidays, you also mentioned that one could not do any house chores or engage in any farming, so could you tell us which chores, which jobs could be performed and which couldn't during those -- on those religious holidays?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was your Slava or some other holiday, for instance, one should not build a house or do any gardening, work in a shop or a hostelry. I mean that has nothing to do with it and one can do it any day. Or you can wash, you can clean, but on your Slava, on your saint's day, on your family saint's day, you shouldn't really do any housework or anything else. You are there to meet your guests, to entertain your guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groome asked you about what Mitar Vasiljevic did after 1992, what was his job then, and you did say something like that he worked for a while and then stopped. Could you please be more precise? There are different ways of not working, that is, there is a paid leave, unpaid leave, or notice, that is being unemployed. So what happened? Did he quit, did he take a leave, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar was on an unpaid leave because there were no salaries to mention and he was -- he had nowhere to go, that is, there were no salaries. There was just a little bit of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what did that mean, by statute? What does an unpaid leave mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be on an unpaid leave means that you are still formally employed; that is, your years of service are still included, but you don't go to work and you don't get any salary, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does this mean that his company paid all the fringe benefits, except that he did not have to go to work, and at the same time he received no remuneration, since it was an unpaid leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. He did not go to work, but they paid his social insurance, his health insurance, his pension insurance, but he did not get any salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But did it happen once in a while that they would invite him back and that he would work, nevertheless, for a shorter or a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went in case of a wedding or some party or some celebration, something like that; otherwise he didn't. When there was more work involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When Mr. Groome asked you about his revenue at the time, considering the situation, you literally said, "He served at weddings and dispatches." So will you please explain to us what do you mean by these dispatches, or sendings-off, and what are these parties and what are these festivities and how could he work there? Was it private? Who organised those, and how could he work there?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one still does that. Mitar was usually invited privately, and he usually didn't charge for that if it was a close relative; distant relatives, and of course from people who were complete strangers. People usually invite very many people, very many guests to these send-offs, up to 500 people, so then he would go to work there. And as I said, if it was any of the relatives, then he wouldn't charge them anything, but otherwise, if it was somebody strange and unrelated, then he would charge for that. Of course, I have very few relatives, so he didn't work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And on such occasions, when he did this privately, would he be paid only in money, in cash, or would it sometimes be in kind too; that is, would he be given perhaps some foodstuffs in remuneration?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends. If, for instance, the chief host works abroad and he has lots of money, then of course he would pay cash; if not, then he would give him perhaps drink or meat, things like that. It depended. A shirt, perhaps, depending on what the host could afford.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand, it varied, one case to the other, depending on who organised this party, and then he decided whether and what he would charge?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So he also -- he went to work at different fairs too, privately?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. He went around fairs. Yes, he organised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Perhaps because this is yet another tradition and it doesn't exist in all the countries all around the world, could you please explain what is a fair and what do you do there, so that we could see what is it that he could do there to make some money.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a fair is a country fair, where many people get together, where you sing and dance. Usually when something is being opened, for instance, a church or a new school, then lots of people will get together and there is a lot of food and drink going around, and Mitar would take care of this catering, of the whole catering for such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And such fairs, apart from such events, that is, a new church or a new school being inaugurated, would such fairs be organised on some religious holidays too?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Usually there would be such big celebrations, big dos for religious holidays. It was before the war and during the war too. Easter, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, a few moments ago you were answering Mr. Groome and said that when it came to Mitar Vasiljevic's behaviour, he suffered a great deal when he saw wounded and crippled persons around him. So my question is -- my question has to do with him as a host, as the lord of the house. When he gets ready for a holiday, when you slaughter poultry or a lamb or a pig, does the host himself do it, and did Mitar Vasiljevic do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the custom is, yes, to slaughter a lamb or a pig, but Mitar could never do that and we had to ask one of our neighbours to do it. I remember well when SFOR lived in our house, they wanted to celebrate something and they wanted to have a roast lamb, and then we asked a neighbour to do that, because Mitar could never bring himself up to slaughtering a lamb or chicken or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But was that, otherwise, a custom or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it was, for every Slava. Always one would have either a lamb or a pig or something. But Mitar could never slaughter them. We usually asked one of the neighbours or his father or somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether it was a custom to have that as one of the courses. My question was: Isn't it customary for the father of the family to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, that is so, but since Mitar could never bring himself to do anything like that, then we always asked somebody else to do that, whether it be a chicken or a lamb or a pig or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also mentioned that his father did that too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He either asks his father, or his father simply does it. But Mitar never did it. Mitar never slaughtered any animal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because he was averse to it. He didn't like to do that. He simply did not like that. He was bothered by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one more question. When it comes to the place about which Mr. Groome asked you, and that is where he had been injured, did -- after that, did Mitar ever take you to that site and show you that place, or is it that you learned about it from his stories and from what other witnesses told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I never really went to this spot, but that he ever took me to the place and showed it to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I assume you know the area quite well. A moment ago you told us that you worked on the square. So was it that square, is it, that you worked, somewhere near the place where he fell?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I worked nearby, but because he had gone to the hospital, nobody ever showed it to me. Sometimes as we would pass by, Mitar would say, "Well, yes, that's where I fell," but that he ever took me to the exact spot and pointed at it and said, "That's where I fell," no, he never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, I would like to ask you: Did people in the shop where you used to work in 1992 ever discuss the death of Mrs. Bahija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear really. Could you repeat, please? I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My question is: Did people in the shop you used to work at in 1992 ever discuss the death of Mrs. Bahija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know whether she's alive or dead. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Did you go to the Uzice hospital on the same day when you received a telephone call about the injury of your husband?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't go the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Why you didn't go on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have a car and I had small children, so I had to find somebody to look after them and until I found somebody who would be with my children and where -- to whom to take them, I could not go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But you said you received the telephone call approximately at 8.00 so if you had any intention to go to, it was possible to go to the Uzice hospital on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I would have managed to find a car that night or something. I don't know whether there was any kind of public transport. I don't think there was any public transport at the time to go through Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: When you went to the Uzice hospital, you went by car?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went by car when I took Mitar out of the hospital. Otherwise -- well, I don't know. At times it could have been that I went by bus and perhaps sometimes I went by car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: How many minutes did it take to go to the Uzice hospital from your house or from the centre of Visegrad approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the means of transportation. It depends whether there are any delays, whether it's a bus that you're taking or a car. Well, I think about two hours. I think at least two hours. I think that now if you take a bus, then it would take you two hours now, but at that time there were many delays because the war was on at the time so I don't really know how long it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Your house is close to the house of Dragan Tomic, the commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's the same street, about 100, 200 metres away from our place. We have to pass by his house on our way to the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: How do you characterise the relationship of Mitar Vasiljevic with Dragan Tomic, the commander of the police? It was good, intimate or other; how do you characterise?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic was a very, very nice man. So we were on good terms with him always. Mitar, I don't know, all of us, we were all on good terms with him. He was a very nice man indeed. I can tell you only all the best about him. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Your husband Mitar Vasiljevic had particularly good relationship with Dragan Tomic, other than the other neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why of course. I mean they were on very good terms like everybody else was. Everybody was friendly with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you any questions arising out of that, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one, Your Honour and it has to do with the question of whether there was a house across the street from the Vasiljevic house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Perhaps in view of some other explanations, I should like to ask Mrs. Vasiljevic to explain if across the street from their house. Are there any houses there and if not, then why?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, across the street from my house, no. Next to my house is the creek and there's Dr. Dragan's house. And across, opposite from our house is the Drina so there can't be any other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. In the street, the houses are on only one side of the street because on the other side of the street borders on the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, for the evidence you have given and for coming here to give that evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, we've got your list of witnesses for next week. You will recall that when we were discussing Friday of next week, and I told you that there was a plenary meeting of the Judges in the morning that we would give you the afternoon off depending upon the speed with which we have been travelling. Now, I have to say that we have not been travelling as quickly as I had anticipated. I think that in those circumstances, we will certainly resume the trial next Friday after the Judges have finished their meeting. It may mean that you may have to wait a little while seeing we have six new judges. I don't know how long they're going to talk for, if they're going to talk at all, but at the moment, it is due to start at 9.30, I think, and I suggest that you be ready to proceed at 11.30 and we'll certainly fill in the rest of the morning and the afternoon, certainly we'll be hearing evidence. So you better get some more witnesses along for next week. I'd do that, and I should explain this, as I think I have indicated before. We are under a very strict time constraint in relation to this trial. It was stated that we would finish it this year and I have a terrible feeling at the moment that we will not unless we spend every moment of the time available with the trial. Of course depending upon Mr. Groome's response to the questions I asked him yesterday, it could be that there will be less witnesses to be called, but at this stage, I must assume that the Prosecution case is as it was opened which, unfortunately, will require you to call the eight witnesses who will simply say that your client was in hospital in Uzice. Well, now, I don't think it's worth while trying to start another witness now. We will resume again at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will be shown the pseudonym we'll be referring to you, as we're not going to be using your name and surname. Could you please tell us whether your real name is on the piece of paper that the usher is going to now show you and that your number is VGD23.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's your next number as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. My concern is I know what the last one was, but you may reserve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit -- D24 and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: VGD23, I'm going to start my examination-in-chief, and I'd like to ask you your particulars, but when you tell us, could you be careful not to jeopardise your protected identity. Could you tell us where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Strazbenice, the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I am 46 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What education do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I completed secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where and when did you begin working after you had completed your education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That was in 1976. I started working in Visegrad, [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you live and work in Visegrad from that time until the present day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the same institution from 1976 to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you worked in the [redacted] from 1976, I should like to ask you to explain the following: If you look at the period up until 1990 or 1991, how did the police force function? What was the set-up, and were there any differences, especially from that period to the spring of 1992? Could you tell us briefly something about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: From 1976, right up until about the time that the national parties were formed, the work of the police force was based partially - not partially - almost 100 per cent, I would say, on the rules and regulations governing the police force and police procedure. However, for the period that followed that, I couldn't claim that that was true. I omitted to answer one of your questions, I think. Let me say that I worked in a [redacted] [redacted], and a third of them were Serbs and two-thirds of the policemen there were Muslims, which more or less reflected the percentage and ratio of the ethnic groups in Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So at that time, the national composition of the municipality was in that ratio, and this was reflected in the police force as well; is that right? That is right, I take it. Now, were there any special problems? When I say "problems," I don't mean the standard type of thing one encounters in a police force, but in a nationalistic sense, before the multiparty elections.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of any drastic example of anything like that, any internationality or interethnic -- how can I call that? - excessive behaviour or anything like that during that period. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you say that the work of the police force at that time, given the multi-ethnic composition, was effective, efficient, and no problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I claim that with full responsibility. Yes, it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us now something a little more about the state of affairs after the multiparty elections took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was the situation like then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, with the formation of the national parties themselves, the SDA to begin with, there was a disruption, an upset, and -- of interethnic relations and this was reflected in the police station as well. Some things began to happen which were absolutely foreign to us until that time. We weren't accustomed to those kinds of things taking place, at least not in the environment in which I had lived and work up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, or rather can you give us an example which would be characteristic for those types of changes in the relationships that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, let me start with the formation of the nationalist parties themselves. There was public rallying of citizens when the parties were established, and a change took place, the security and traffic regulation, for example, and the regulation of other affairs which comes under the exclusive competence and authority of the police force began to be organised on a self-initiative basis. They began to organise their own services. And then traffic signs were destroyed, graffiti was predominant, posters were stuck up haphazardly over shop windows and the facades of houses and in other visible prominent spots on the roads as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. well. Later on, the first more serious excesses and incidents took place which largely disrupted and upset interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before I ask you something about that, about the outbursts and excessive behaviour, can you tell us something that you just said, you mentioned graffiti, posters stuck on the walls of houses and buildings, what kind of graffiti? What kind of posters? What was written on them which could lead and cause this disruption? What were they about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: At the beginning, there was graffiti which glorified the party concerned, that is to say, the SDA party and appealed to its members to vote for it. But later on, this grew into graffiti which were threatening in nature and they were addressed to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The first point you made is certainly something that is allowed, that is to say, parties can advertise themselves in the way you have described, but what you said occurred later on, I'd like to hear a bit more about that, please. What happened later on? Because you said that there were some graffiti addressed to the Serb people, what slogans were written up this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you quotations now, but actually it said, "Serbs, what are you waiting for, Chetniks?" They were insulting slogans. "What are you looking for in these regions?" And things like that, "What are you doing here?" And so on. There were lots of others too. One of them was one which said, "It's not 1941 anymore." Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Slogans, graffiti, posters of this kind, did they have an effect on interethnic relations and disrupt them; that is to say, how did the Serbs take to these things in Visegrad? What did they think of them? What was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, messages and slogans of this kind wouldn't be well-received by anybody and so the Serb people were not happy to see them. They felt the Serb people felt jeopardised, threatened in a way. And later on, the Serb Democratic Party was established, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which party was formed first in Visegrad after the multiparty elections -- rather prior to the multiparty elections, which party was formed first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: In Visegrad, the first party to be formed was the Party of Democratic Action or the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To the best of your recollections, how soon after that -- how long after that was the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite remember, but certainly -- well, I can only give you an approximation. Several months went by before, so not the following month, but maybe even six months later. I can't give you an exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. At the time, did any parties exist or were they operating that were not national parties, ones which tried to maintain the interethnic community and who had members of the different ethnicities, both ethnicities, in fact, as their members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. That was the SDP party, and I think, as if I remember correctly, that the SDP had a rally at the sports centre and I think that took place before the SDS party was formed. And also in Visegrad, there was the Reformist Party of Ante Markovic, I think that's what was its name, and that party too had supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, the two parties that you mentioned, those last two, were they successful in the multiparty elections, especially for the Visegrad area, as far as Visegrad is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: They, that is to say the number of voters, came after the national parties which means that the order was the SDA, the SDS, and then the rest, the other parties. The SDA, the SDS and then the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The order you stated, was that the majority vote, does it -- do you mean that the SDA won the elections, the multiparty elections? Did they get the most number of votes in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you were talking about a moment ago about graffiti and posters and the fact that they created tensions, does that relate to the time before the elections or after the elections, or both those periods, both before and after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I think that the problem became more serious after the advent of the SDA party, after the SDA party came to power in Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in your opinion, it was after the elections and the arrival of the SDA in Visegrad that the situation deteriorated. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was much, much more marked than it had been in the pre-electoral period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You explained to us a moment ago that before the elections, that prior to the elections, in the police force, the ratio of policemen reflected the national structure or ethnic structure of the municipality itself and that everything functioned properly. Now, was there a similar ratio in the other government organs, local organs of power and authority in Visegrad? I'm talking about the period before the multiparty elections now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. The posts and functions were distributed according to what we used to call the key, the national ratio, or national key, we used to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, could you explain what the national key meant? Did it mean proportionate representation of a certain nation or ethnic group on the territory, or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: The percentage composition of the municipality according to the national structure was represented both in the organs and institutions that existed in the municipality and the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could we say in more simple terms that it was a -- that two-thirds of the population -- that two-thirds of the cadres were Muslims, according to that key, and one-third of the cadres were Serbs, according to the national figures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about after the multiparty elections, when the new authorities came into being? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: According to the electoral results, the results of the first multiparty elections, the SDA party in Visegrad had an assembly majority of over half, and then this parity ratio was upset in the government. I think that at the first assembly, when the multiparty assembly was actually set up, outside legal procedures that had been established earlier on, and bypassing those procedures, a vote was taken, and there was an ordinary majority vote in the Municipal Assembly, by a simple majority, which meant that absolute power was taken over by the SDA. There was a simple majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I followed you, what you're saying is that there was a change in the statute of the municipality, stating -- with a simple majority. Does that mean that there should have been a qualified majority, that some other two-thirds majority vote was needed, or some other, and that the new authorities did not respect that? Is that what you're saying? Did I understand you to say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. Up until then, there was always a two-thirds majority vote that carried, and that was in line with the Statute of the Municipal Assembly. However, on that occasion, everybody said there was an illegal procedure that was applied, and what was introduced was a simple majority vote, which meant 51 votes, 50 plus 1, 51 votes as a simple majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this referred to questions and issues that had to be solved by a two-thirds majority vote before that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what this led up to? Give us some characteristic examples of the repercussions that this establishment of power had, in brief terms, if you're able to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: With the establishment of the new government, the new authorities, we saw the first unfortunate events unfolding. One of the most drastic examples which I wish to stress was that Serbs were stopped in their cars. They were pulled out of their cars, they were beaten on the spot; that is to say, they were physically attacked. Next, buses would be stopped which were coming from Serbia proper. The passengers would be ill-treated. Then military vehicles would be stopped and the soldiers would be mistreated. They would be physically attacked. Then killings took place. That is to say, the killing of a Serb took place in a village. The village was Crncici. The Serb flag was burnt on Visegrad square, and policemen were held prisoner in the police station if they were Serbs. They were detained in the station. People opened fire on the police station. Firearms were used. Barricades or roadblocks were set up along the certain roads and roads leading up to the settlements, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, Judge Janu wants to clear something up about what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Just to understand what was said before Mr. Domazet, would you be so kind and clarify it for the Chamber what was the character of the electoral system of the country at that time was that electoral system changed before the multiparty elections or was the electoral -- was the electoral system the same before multiparty elections and after or was it changed? That's my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will ask the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I suppose you understood that question. Will you tell us if before the multiparty elections, the electoral system, they took any change, that is, as applied to Visegrad, did the -- was the municipal statute that you mentioned changed before the multiparty elections or after them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: If you are referring to the ratios or rather the two-third decision making or just simple majority voting, this particular change took place afterwards; that is, in that regard, this statute was changed following the multiparty elections. When the assembly was constituted ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's try this way. So the new local authority that was set up following the outcome of the elections, did they find their statute in force according to which important matters, matters relative to ethnic equality were to be settled by two-thirds majority and that the new assembly then changed it into a simple majority; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That's right. The new assembly changed that and said that simple majority, that is, 50 plus one vote were sufficient to take decisions on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My question led to another point because in our system, there is an electoral law for the general elections and electoral law for the municipal elections and my question was: Was this change which the assembly -- after the municipal assembly after the multiparty elections has done, was it the change of general law passed by the parliament of the country, or was it just change which the assembly could have done by its own authority? So maybe the witness is not able to explain it to me, but to have all this evidence and to be able to evaluate it, this is a crucial point. You both are lawyers, so you understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, witness, I suppose you understood that question, but do you know the answer to it; that is, were the changes due to the changes adopted and approved by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know if that went in line with the changes that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina either prior to or following the multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: The municipal statute is adopted by the municipal assembly and the municipal assembly is the one which changes the statute, that is, the councilmen at the municipal, at the session of the municipal assembly. In other words, the republic and the state parliament does not impose the municipal statutes of the municipalities but, on the other hand, these statutes must be in conformity with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that, I think, was the purpose of the question. Was the constitution changed to this effect which would then allow the change -- this change in the statute? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I think not. Because had that been done, it wouldn't have been unlawful, and I did point out that this change of statute was not lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you did that, but shall I say that is what the Serb side, if I may call it that, thought of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'd like you to go back again to that period of time, that is, the new government, but in the police in which you continued working. Will you tell us briefly how did this new authority affect the work of the police and then extending it to the general interethnic relations in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: When the new assembly was constituted, and when the already mentioned decision-making system was introduced, it was bound to find its reflection in the police station as well. The cadres were changed, that is, the executives were new. The former chief of the public security station who was a Serb, he was removed and replaced by an SDA man, and that is a man who was a Muslim, that is, man number one in the police station was now a Muslim. The Serb officers, not only Serb, I'm sure, but Muslim too who had been doing their work professionally until then were -- also fell victims, if I may put it that way, of that new authority, that is, individuals were dismissed and assigned to lower-ranking posts or lost their jobs altogether. And that was a tool of, if I may call it that, that is, those people were unassigned, that is, they were receiving their salaries but they did not come to work and they were called unassigned personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean after the change and after the change of government, that many Serb policemen, but not only Serb, Muslim too, those who were good professionals, that they were removed or demoted or rather that they did not perform the jobs any longer even though they continued getting their salaries; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, it was only, at least in my police station, it affected only the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, tell me about this: Weapon permits, even hunting weapons and ammunition and all that, that fell under the jurisdiction of the police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did the situation in this field change too? We know that this is a particularly sensitive area, especially in a multiethnic environment such as Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a briefing at which -- and this was one of the items on the agenda of that briefing, what had happened -- well, I'm not quite sure, but of about 105 applications resolved over a period of time, 100 were -- concerned the applicants who were Muslims and negligible part of applications resolved and approved came from Serbs and the same held true of the applications for the purchase of firearms and permits for the purchase of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned these figures, does this mean not applications submitted but applications which were resolved in the affirmative way? Is that people who were authorised, who were allowed to buy their weapons or ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes. These were the applications that were granted, these applications for the purchase and licences for weapons and ammunition were the ones which were granted. There must have been more applications than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And at that time, was there unlawful arming of people? Did you receive any information about that in your police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I am sure that, yes, people were arming themselves unlawfully, because from time to time one could hear fire open from various firearms, in all parts of the municipality. One could hear whole rounds of fire, so that it was easy to infer from that that somebody was procuring weapons unlawfully, because automatic weapons cannot be bought by anyone legally, lawfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you personally, and your [redacted], did you take any steps in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Nothing special was done, and even, although we had received information that some policemen were participating in the distribution of these unlawful weapons and ammunition, even then, nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those policemen about which you had learnt that they were participating in that, were they Muslims or Serbs, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Muslims. On one occasion they were caught red-handed taking the ammunition from the police station. Yes, taking the ammunition from the depot in the -- from the storage room in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they then arrested and was the investigation undertaken against them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, they were not arrested and no proceedings were launched, even though we knew exactly who they were; that is, we knew their full names. The Ministry of the Interior was notified about this, and that was when the first major misunderstandings between policemen who were Serbs and policemen who were Muslims began. A group had come to a briefing, because after that incident, Serb policemen - [redacted]- after that incident, Serb policemen refused to go on working with policemen who had been caught red-handed, that is, illegally taking away, or rather, simply stealing the ammunition from the storage room in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it then that the Serb police separated, parted company with the Muslim part of the police? We've already heard here about this from some other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: And then a period of time ensued when the Serb policemen did not come to work. We requested that the policemen who had done that be disciplined and be removed from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did this happen or not? Tell me, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned as one of many incidents the capture of Serb policemen. Will you now, please, as briefly as possible, will you tell us who did that, when did it happen, and what was it all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, this is precisely the material which you said was going to be dealt with very generally, and although you continue to use the word "briefly" in your questions, the answers are anything but brief. Now, the relevance of it has never been made clear. I understand you want to get this witness through by the end of the afternoon. You're not going to get anywhere near it if you continue with this irrelevant material. We are concerned with the attacks upon the Bosnian Muslim civilian population, not with the attacks upon the Bosnian Serbian civilian population. It's a matter for you, but it seems to me that you have gone way beyond what you said you were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only a few more questions, because the witness is well informed about these events. And the incident I just mentioned is something that happened on the eve of the Uzice Corps arrival, that is, precisely at that time, and many witnesses of the Prosecution tried to somehow disregard these events, and all I wanted this witness to do was explain it to us. We have another witness who is protected. I'd like to show the name of this witness to this witness because I'll have to refer to him and I do not want to mention his name. But I only have a few questions more for this witness and then I will be over. This should be VGD25. I should like to tender it into evidence and I'd like to have one copy of this shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: VGD25. Is that going to be Exhibit D25, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D25, and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you had a look at the name of this witness? If you want to mention him, then please refer to him under the number indicated next to him, which is VGD61 [as interpreted]. Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, I did. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
