utterances.text: Was he involved in any of the incidents which took place at that time, which is April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: As far as I know, in April 1992, when the conflict broke out, VGD25, [redacted] [redacted], [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: According to eyewitnesses, that same evening -- that same day, in the evening of that same day, as day set, he fled to a locality which was ethnically Muslim and where he anyway worked, because, that is, he was the leader of the sector, for that particular sector. In other words, his job assignment was there and he knew people in that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that was the locality of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Medjedja, it is a neighbourhood community comprising several hamlets. So it is the neighbourhood community of Medjedja with a number of hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And just one more question, related question, do you recall if he was called to account, if he was ever brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, he was never brought before court nor have ever any steps been taken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And outside of all of that and respective of all these situations, let me ask you, did you know or do you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I know Mitar Vasiljevic. I've known him for some 30 years or so, 25, 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to see him in May/June 1992? Did you hear anything about him at that time in view of your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: At that time, I was performing my job in the field so that I wasn't all that often in the town itself, but my wife who is a salesperson in the centre of the town, in a shop there, told me that sometime in mid-June, thereabouts, he had organised the cleaning of the town. My wife was one of those who took part in that cleaning of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you never saw him at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That's right. I did not see him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I do not have any further questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that the ELMO just be pushed back a bit. I can't see the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in connection with your duties [redacted], did you ever have occasion to accompany convoys of Muslims who wished to leave the area? Did you ever do that perhaps to provide protection for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I did once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that was or when that was, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes, it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was -- were these Muslims leaving voluntarily or were they being forced to leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: As far as I saw, and the convoy that I accompanied, escorted, it was women, children, and elderly persons who were voluntarily, they voluntarily wanted to leave Visegrad and go to Central Bosnia because probably they felt safer there because I, too, had sent my children to Serbia and left them with relatives because I thought that they'd be safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was I correct in thinking that you accompanied this convoy to protect them? Is that why you accompanied this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That was my job to ensure the security of these people with the other members of the escort, that is to say, to escort them safely and securely through Serb settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, why did they need to be protected as they travelled through Serb settlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: At that time in those parts, there were paramilitary units or groups. So not only was there a threat from those quarters to a Muslim convoy, but it was a threat to the Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question: At some point during this period, checkpoints were set up all around the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't see them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say in your job [redacted] you travelled around the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: During that period, I was not performing my usual [redacted]. I was positioned more on roads providing security, and the main road, you know, runs through Visegrad. There are a number of regional roads and local roads so that mostly I was providing security for those roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you saw somebody on one of the roads that you are protecting and that person does not have -- I'm sorry, and you do not recognise this person, would you ask to see this person's identification papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't, unless he were armed or something like that. I don't know everybody, so if -- unless somebody is suspicious in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me come back to my earlier question. Since you were one of the people protecting the roads, you, better than anybody, should know whether or not at any time during this period, there were checkpoints along those roads. At any time during the summer, spring and summer of 1992, were there checkpoints along the roads in and out of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to come back to this convoy that you escorted. Can you give us an idea of how many people, how many women, children, elderly altogether, about how many people were in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: There were three buses and two trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how many police were with you protecting that convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Not all of us were policemen. Everybody providing the convoy's security, members providing security for the convoy, there were ten of us, which meant two for each vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea of how many of those ten were policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I can't even remember the names of those ten, but as far as I recall, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I take it from your answer that you do not remember the names of the other men who were with you protecting that convoy, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Well, I know four or five of them. Do you want me to start enumerating? I don't know all their names, but four or five, because nine years have gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I understand. If you could give us the five, we'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: There was Andric who died later, who was killed later on. There were two Simsic men, there was Goran.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us Goran's last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Nedic. He didn't work as a policeman, he was one of the staff at the police station before the war, an employee of the police station but not a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: [redacted], were you the person who organised the security for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No. I didn't organise it. We were assigned the duty of providing security for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who assigned you that duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I was assigned that duty by the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other men who weren't policemen, were they armed during this duty to protect this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who issued them these automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't answer that. I don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you escorting the convoy to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: The convoy was going from Visegrad, via Rogatica and Sokolac and Knezina, towards Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Olovo, it's actually a mountain, the place called Mount Olovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Olovo is a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your duties as a [redacted], did you ever have to arrest Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I never received orders like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, surely at some point in time, protecting the security of the roads and the town, you must have arrested somebody who was doing something illegally, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: If you mean criminals, then yes, but they weren't extremists. They are two different concepts in our country, extremists and criminal, two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many -- or what would be an average number of criminals who were Muslims would you arrest per month during this time period, April to August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: From April 1992 to what month? I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a single occasion to arrest anyone, to arrest a Muslim during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever given the responsibility of supervising the detention of Muslim criminals or extremists who may have been arrested during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time when you became aware that the SDS party was distributing weapons to Serbs in and around Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, never. I never learnt information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you learned such information, would you have acted upon it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I would write an informative report to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a few minutes ago about paramilitaries in the area. Were these Muslim paramilitaries, Serb paramilitaries, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: My claim was not based on my own personal observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've given us a rather extensive overview of the situation in Visegrad and your beliefs regarding the cause of the problems in Visegrad. I want to read you a portion of a statement by another Serb just like yourself, approximately the same age as you, and ask you, is this not a more accurate account of how the problems occurred in Visegrad: "In the early part of April of 1992, Perisic Risto, one of the leaders of the SDS and the head of the public security station, met with this Serb witness and said that he was going to ask the Uzice Corps to intervene in Visegrad. On the 12th of April, 1992, Perisic Risto led approximately 3.000 soldiers from the Uzice Corps into Visegrad. These troops were joined by the volunteer units led by Jeftic Dejan." Do you know that man, Jeftic Dejan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Continuing: "His unit consisted of approximately 30 soldiers. Two to three days later, Lukic Milan arrived in Visegrad with his unit of approximately 15 men. Fifteen more men joined this group, including Vasiljevic Mitar, Lukic Sredoje, Vujicic Niko," and it says "a brother of Lukic Milan, Knezevic Mitar, Trifkovic Miroslav, aka Miki, Markovic Mladen, Tanaskovic Nenad, Gorazdak," and that's a nickname. "When they arrived, the plunder and destruction of houses began." Sir, isn't that a more accurate account of how the problems in Visegrad began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is: Isn't that a more truthful account of how the problems in Visegrad began in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: In my opinion, no, because the Uzice Corps was not that small for one man to be able to call it and bring it to Visegrad. It numbered 3.000. That is not a serious statement. Now, anybody who attended the media was quite clear. People knew in Visegrad and the surroundings that not only Visegrad, but downstream - Bajna Basta, Zvornik, and all the other places - that they were threatened with a catastrophe in case of the waters being released, or that Murat Sabanovic should release the waters from the reservoir of the hydroelectric power station. So I took that to be very serious, and anybody who saw what water could do and what water did when a part of it was released from the reservoir would have been quite clear as to why the Uzice Corps had been sent to Visegrad, because there was the serious threat that Murat would release the waters from the reservoir and that this would cause a material and human and ecological catastrophe. So in my opinion, that was the only reason for which this was done, and straight away, afterwards -- actually, they didn't stay on too long. They left soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VGD23, let's go back to the convoy. Was anybody -- was any of the Muslims -- were any of them hurt on their trip to Olovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: At the time, the passengers got off, got out. That is to say, when we had reached our destination, the line -- at Sokolac, we were given a guide, two guides, and they were in the first bus with me. And when we arrived at our destination point, it was a large space, an open space where the vehicles were turned around, and the people started getting out, off the buses and off the trucks. So at that point, from the elevated areas -- from the hills, surrounding hills, shooting started from different weapons, and the targets were the buses and trucks. The passengers from the convoy who had already got off laid down on the ground, on the grass and on the road, and we, under fire, managed to pull out towards -- as I was in the first bus. Later on, I wasn't able to get into the same bus, the first bus, but I boarded the last bus afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many women, children, and elderly died on this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: From the injuries sustained, two people died.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you a portion of that statement of someone who was on that bus, I will ask you at the end of it, is this not a more accurate description of what happened. "In mid-June of 1992, during the ethnic cleansing of Visegrad and surroundings, [redacted] and others escorted six buses and two trucks with Muslims leaving the area. The convoy stopped near Olovo and some of the Bosniaks tried to run, run away into the woods. The escort of Bosnian Serb nationality started shooting and one woman and a child were killed while another child was wounded." The witness then says they saw you, [redacted], Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic, and Nenad Tanaskovic. You five men were the men who were shooting at these people isn't that, in fact, what occurred on that day when you escorted these people out from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That's not true. None of that is true. I see no reason why they would not confirm my statement, Asim Nuhanovic, Sevala Veletovac I think the surname was, Hecimovic, a neighbour whom I knew. Hamdo was the father's name of this Hecimovic man, I can't remember his first name. I'm quite certain that they would confirm my statement and not the one you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were the people that I mentioned, were they present at this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I say with full responsibility that none of the people that you read out were. Dragan Tomic only in Visegrad gave me the task of -- gave me this assignment and stayed in Visegrad. Now, as to the others that you mentioned from the list you read out, I say with full responsibility that none of them was in the convoy nor anywhere near the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How do you know her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I know her from secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know that she was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what car she drove?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am in possession of a statement from July of 1992 which, although it does not claim that you killed Behija Zukic, it said that you were the person who ordered the murder of Behija Zukic. Is it a fact that you ordered the murder of Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: That's not true, nor would I ever be able to give anybody such an order. That's -- just a normal person could not even think of doing anything like that let alone -- that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever present on the bridge in Visegrad when there was a shooting and some Muslims were injured? Were you ever present during that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: I was never present, not only on the bridge but anywhere else, at some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know somebody by the name of Ibrasim Kesmer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: Ibrisim?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: What about the surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Kesmer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD23
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm in possession of a statement which alleges that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, how long do you think you are going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would imagine about 20, 25 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, what is the problem with this witness? I was only just told that you had hoped to get him back to the former Yugoslavia this afternoon. Can he be brought back later?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is due to leave tomorrow morning. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that. All I'm saying is: Can he be brought back at the end of next week or some other time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he can. If necessary, he can come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if the cross-examination can be concluded, and on a Friday afternoon, it is very unfair to ask the crew here to stay on for what could be, despite Mr. Groome's estimate, a very long time. So I'm afraid you'll have to come back later to conclude your evidence. I regret that we can't finish it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we ask the witness, while he is here, two things: Whether he absolutely must leave tomorrow, which means that he would have to come back, or can we ask him if he could defer travelling and stay until Monday, and perhaps we could continue him on Monday. Perhaps it's a bigger problem for him to go and come back. So may we ask him that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's up to the witness. I don't propose to order him to do one thing or the other. Which is more convenient, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well as I am here, perhaps it would be better for me to stay on until Monday and to continue on Monday so that we complete the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the best way of dealing with it, we'll deal with it that way. We'll adjourn now until 9.30 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
